video.title: How Scap Retraction Powers the One-Handed Backhand

classification.reason: The coach explains the biomechanics of scapular retraction, pull slot positioning, wrist stabilization, and grip alignment for the one-handed backhand.

problem.title_as_question: How does scapular retraction power the one-handed backhand?
problem.definition: Players struggle to hit a powerful and fault-tolerant one-handed backhand when they fail to pull with their upper back from the proper slot, let their wrist break through contact, or hold the racket with a slanted grip.

symptoms.description: Player initiates the pull too close to the body and stomach rather than out in front in the pull slot.
The wrist breaks freely and backward right through the hitting zone, causing string angle instability.
Player rotates farther than intended with the torso and shanks the ball.
Player feels inability to generate pulling force and strains weaker arm muscles like deltoids and triceps.
Player holds the racket with knuckles slanted at a 135-degree angle rather than perpendicular to the handle.

causes.statement: The string angle does not stay consistent through the hitting zone because of erratic wrist movement.
The player completely relaxes the hand and allows the wrist to freely break through contact.
The grip lacks a 90-degree orthogonal relationship between forearm and handle, causing the wrist to break sideways.
The player sets up the pull slot too late and close to the stomach, pulling sideways rather than back to front.
The upper back rhomboids and traps are not engaged in scapular retraction to drive the racket forward.
The player pulls with only one hand instead of executing a two-handed guided pull into the slot.

angles.summary: Scapular retraction pulls the shoulder blades together using the rhomboids and trapezius to create back-to-front drive.
Testing static pulling force at the chosen pull slot against resistance confirms if the body position can generate power.
Unlike the forehand where wrist break naturally happens after contact, the backhand wrist will break through contact if left completely loose.
Forearm rotation around the long axis that keeps string angle stable is required, while wrist breaking perpendicular to contact must be resisted.
The grip must maintain a 90-degree orthogonal angle between the forearm and handle to enable proper forearm whip without wrist break.
Good players use a compact, non-whippy block swing with fixed wrist angle on difficult shots like serve returns.

solutions.summary: Pull the shoulder blades together using the rhomboids and trapezius muscles to drive through the shot from back to front.
Set up at the pull slot against a wall or in space and test whether you can generate pulling force from your upper back.
solutions.external_goal: The wall or pull slot position

solutions.summary: Keep the non-dominant hand on the racket throat to guide the racket into the pull slot before releasing into the pull.
solutions.external_goal: Guide racket throat with non-dominant hand into pull slot

solutions.summary: Prepare with the racket head pointed down, pull through contact with fixed wrist angle, and only add dynamic racket preparation as comfort grows.
solutions.external_goal: Prepare with racket head pointed down

solutions.summary: Verify that the racket handle forms a strict 90-degree orthogonal angle with the forearm and knuckles align parallel along the handle.
solutions.external_goal: Racket handle forming a 90-degree angle with forearm
